concepts.title: Alkyl Halides
concepts.conceptBody:
Properties of Alkyl Halides

Alkyl halides are a class of compound where a halogen atom or atoms are bound to an $\text{s}{{\text{p}}^{3}}$ orbital of an alkyl group.

$\text{CHC}{{\text{l}}_{3}}\text{ (Chlor oform : organic solvent)}$

$\text{C}{{\text{F}}_{2}}\text{C}{{\text{l}}_{2}}\text{ (Freon-12 : refrigerant CFC) }$

$\text{C}{{\text{F}}_{3}}\text{CHClBr (Halothane : anesthetic) }$

Halogen atoms are more electronegative than carbon atoms, and so the $\text{C}-\text{X}$ bond is polarized. Here X stands for halogens.

The $\text{C}-\text{X}$ bond is polarized in such a way that there is partial positive charge on the carbon and partial negative charge on the halogen.

Electronegativity decreases in the order of:

$\text{F}>\text{Cl}>\text{Br}>\text{I}$

Carbon-halogen bond lengths increase in the order of:

$\text{C}-\text{F}<\text{C}-\text{Cl}<\text{C}-\text{Br}<\text{C}-\text{I}$

Bond Dipole Moments decrease in the order of:

$\begin{array}{*{35}{l}} \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\text{C}-\text{Cl}\,\,\,\,\,> & \text{C}-\text{F} & > & \text{C}-\text{Br} & > & \text{C}-\text{I} \\ \mu =1.56\text{D} & 1.51\text{D} & {} & 1.48\text{D} & {} & 1.29\text{D} \\ \end{array}$

Typically the chemistry of alkyl halides is dominated by this effect, and usually results in the $\text{C}-\text{X}$ bond being broken (either in a substitution or elimination process).

This reactivity makes alkyl halides useful chemical reagents.

concepts.title: Nomenclature
concepts.conceptBody:
1. Nomenclature

According to IUPAC, alkyl halides are treated as alkanes with a halogen substituent.

The halogen prefixes are Fluoro-, Chloro-, Bromo- and Iodo-.

Examples:

IUPAC nomenclature of alkyl halides with one halogen in haloalkanes and with two similar halogens is halo alkanes. If the halogens present are different, they are prefixed in alphabetical order.

Often compounds of $\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}{{\text{X}}_{2}}$ type are called methylene halides $\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{C}{{\text{l}}_{2}} \right.$ is methylene chloride). $\text{CH}{{\text{X}}_{3}}$ type compounds are called haloforms. $\left( \text{CH}{{\text{I}}_{3}} \right.$ is iodoform).

$\text{C}{{\text{X}}_{4}}$ type compounds are called carbon tetrahalides. $\left( \text{C}{{\text{F}}_{4}} \right.$ is carbon tetrafluoride). Alkyl halides can be primary (1), secondary (2) or tertiary (3).

Other types: 

A geminal (gem) dihalide has two halogens on the same carbon.

A vicinal dihalide has halogen on adjacent carbon atoms.

concepts.title: By Free Radical Halogenation of Alkanes
concepts.conceptBody:
Preparation Of Alkyl Halides

Radical Halogenation of Alkanes 

The one big limitation of this method (especially chlorination) is that it almost inevitably leads to a (often complex) mixture of products. Even chlorination of methane gives a mixture:

$\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{4}}+\text{C}{{\text{l}}_{2}}\xrightarrow{light}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{Cl},\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{C}{{\text{l}}_{2}},\text{CHC}{{\text{l}}_{3}}\text{ and CC}{{\text{l}}_{4}}$

The situation is even worse for the chlorination of alkanes that have more than one kinds of hydrogen:

In the first example, $30%$ of primary halide means that each one of the six primary hydrogens $\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}} \right)$ is responsible for $30%/6=5%$ of product, whereas $70%$ of secondary alkyl halides means that each one of the four secondary hydrogens $\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}} \right)$ is responsible for $70%/4=17.5$ of the product. Hence, chlorination at secondary carbon occurs about 3.5 times the rate of chlorination at primary carbon.

Similarly, in the second example, chlorination occurs at the single tertiary carbon (CH) at about 5 times the rate of chlorination at the primary carbons.

The order of reactivity toward radical chlorination is

$\begin{matrix} {} & R-C{{H}_{3}} & < & {{R}_{2}}C{{H}_{2}} & < & {{R}_{3}}CH \\ {} & 1 & {} & 2 & {} & 3 \\ \text{relative rate} & 1 & {} & 3.5 & {} & 5 \\ \end{matrix}$

This order reflects the relative order of the $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond strengths: $3<2<1$. Since less energy is needed to break a tertiary $\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond than either a 2 or a $1\text{C}-\text{H}$ bond, the resulting tertiary radical is more stable than either a secondary or primary radical.

However, although the rates of chlorination at different carbon atoms are different, the difference is not great, so that in practice, some chlorination occurs at all sites.

concepts.title: Allylic Bromination and Chlorination
concepts.conceptBody:
Radical chlorination has poor selectivity

Bromination, on the other hand, is much more selective, mainly because of the lesser reactivity of the halogen species (in particular $\text{Br}$):

Allylic bromination and chlorination

(Allylic means adjacent to a $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bond)

The bromination of cyclohexene produces a high yield of 3-bromocyclohexene.

An allylic hydrogen has been substituted for a bromine.

  • Compounds with allylic and benzylic hydrogen atoms can be brominated readily using the mild brominating agent N-bromosuccinimide (NBS):

The reaction proceeds via radical substitution method.

One important synthetic consequence of the delocalized allyl radicals is that more than one bromination product is often obtained:

Note: ${{F}_{2}}$ is most reactive while ${{I}_{2}}$ is least reactive. Infact reaction with ${{I}_{2}}$ is reversible and is carried out in the presence of some oxidising agents like $\text{HI}{{\text{O}}_{3}},\text{HN}{{\text{O}}_{3}}$ etc. to oxidise $\text{HI}$.

Some more reactions:

concepts.title: By Alcohols with HBr
concepts.conceptBody:
From alcohols

(1) Using hydrogen halides

$\text{R}-\text{OH}\xrightarrow{H-X}\text{R}-\text{X}$

Some Points:

  • When treated with$\text{HBr}$ or $\text{HCl}$ alcohols typically undergo a nucleophilic substitution reaction to generate an alkyl halide and water.
  • Alcohol relative reactivity order: $3>2>1>$ methyl
  • Hydrogen halide reactivity order: $\text{HI}>\text{HBr}>\text{HCl}>\text{HF}$ (paralleling acidity order).
  • Reaction usually proceeds via an SN1 mechanism which proceeds via a carbocation intermediate, that can also undergo rearrangement.
  • Methanol and primary alcohols will proceed via an SN2 mechanism since these have highly unfavourable carbocations.
  • The reaction of alcohols with $\text{HCl}$ in the presence of $\text{ZnC}{{\text{l}}_{2}}$ (catalyst) forms the basis of the Lucas test for alcohols.

S N 1 mechanism for reaction of Alcohols with $\mathbf{HBr}$

concepts.title: By Reaction of Alcohols with Sulphur and Phosphorus Halides
concepts.conceptBody:
Reaction of alcohols with sulfur and phosphorous halides

Alcohols can be converted to alkyl halides by reaction with thionyl chloride, $\text{SOC}{{\text{l}}_{2}}$; phosphorous trichloride, $\text{PC}{{\text{l}}_{3}}$, phosphorous pentachloride, $\text{PC}{{\text{l}}_{5}}$; or phosphorous tribromide, $\text{PB}{{\text{r}}_{3}}$. For example, ethyl chloride or ethyl bromide can be prepared from ethyl alcohol via reactions with sulfur and phosphorous halides.

Reaction of Alcohol with $\mathbf{PC}{{\mathbf{l}}_{3}}$ 

$3\text{ROH}+\text{PC}{{\text{l}}_{3}}\xrightarrow{{}}\text{RCl}+{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{P}{{\text{O}}_{3}}$

Mechanism:

$\text{HOPC}{{\text{l}}_{2}}$ reacts further to give ${{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{P}{{\text{O}}_{3}}$ and $2\text{RCl}$ molecules.

  • This method is the method because the product formed is gaseous in nature.

$\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{OH}+\text{SOC}{{\text{l}}_{2}}\xrightarrow{\Delta }\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{Cl}+\text{S}{{\text{O}}_{2}}+\text{HCl}$

$\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{OH}+\text{PC}{{\text{l}}_{3}}\xrightarrow{\Delta }\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{Cl}+\text{P}{{(\text{OH})}_{3}}+\text{HCl}$

$\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{OH}+\text{PC}{{\text{l}}_{5}}\xrightarrow{\Delta }\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{Cl}+\text{POC}{{\text{l}}_{3}}+\text{HCl}$

$\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{OH}+\text{PB}{{\text{r}}_{3}}\xrightarrow{\Delta }\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{Br}+\text{P}(\text{OH})_{3}^{+}\text{HBr}$

concepts.title: Reactions of Alkyl Halides
concepts.conceptBody:
Reactions of Alkyl Halides

$\text{RN}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\xrightarrow[-HCl]{RCl}{{\text{R}}_{2}}\text{NH}\xrightarrow{RCl}{{\text{R}}_{3}}~\text{N}\xrightarrow[RCl]{excess}{{\text{R}}_{4}}~{{\text{N}}^{+}}\text{C}{{\text{l}}^{-}}$

Some Basic Terms

(1) The halogen atom may leave with its bonding pair of electrons to give a halide ion which is stable - a halide is called a good leaving group .

(2) If an atom replaces the halide the overall reaction is substitution.

If the halide loss is accompanied by the loss of another atom, the overall reaction is called an elimination .

(3) Very often the other atom lost is a hydrogen (as${{\text{H}}^{+}}$). The elimination of$\text{H}-\text{X}$ is common, and is called a dehydrohalogenation .

Note: Often substitution and elimination reactions will occur in competition with each other.

Mechanism 1

Alcohol first reacts with $\text{SOC}{{\text{l}}_{2}}$ to form an intermediate chlorosulphate ester, which gives alkyl chlorosulphite and $\text{HCl}$. In presence of pyridine, $\text{HCl}$ reacts with it to give pyridinium $\left( \text{Py}{{\text{H}}^{+}} \right)$ion and chloride $\left( \text{C}{{\text{l}}^{-}} \right)$ion. The $\text{C}{{\text{l}}^{-}}$displaces the leaving group $\text{ClSO}_{2}^{-}$and chloro sulphite ester decomposes to $\text{S}{{\text{O}}_{2}},\text{C}{{\text{l}}^{-}}$and $\text{R}-\text{Cl}$ with inversion of configuration.

In the absence of a base and polar solvent, the chlorosulphite ester dissociates into an intimate ion-pair. The $\text{C}{{\text{l}}^{-}}$of the anion of ion-pair attacks from the front side of ${{\text{R}}^{+}}$to give retention of configuration. The retention is observed because $\text{Cl}$ cannot reach the rear of the ${{\text{R}}^{+}}$group but is close to its front side.

This is referred as ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}\text{i}$ (substitution nucleophilic internal) mechanism because a part of the leaving group detaches itself from the rest of the leaving group during the process and attacks the substrate.

concepts.title: Hard Soft Acid Base Theory
concepts.conceptBody:
HSAB Theory (Hard Soft Acid Base theory)

Hard acid : Which has less tendency to accept the lone pair of electrons. For example ${{\text{H}}^{+}}$, $\text{L}{{\text{i}}^{+}},\text{M}{{\text{g}}^{2+}},3$ carbocation.

Soft acid : More tendency to accept pair of electrons. For example $\text{A}{{\text{g}}^{+}},\text{A}{{\text{u}}^{+}},\text{H}{{\text{g}}_{2}}^{2+},\text{C}{{\text{u}}^{2+}}$

Hard base : Which has less tendency to donate lone pair of electrons.

\[\underbrace{{{O}^{2-}},\,\,-{{O}^{-}},\,\,{{N}^{\odot }}}_{({{\text{N}}^{-}}\text{ is a soft base w}\text{.r}\text{.t}\text{. --}{{\text{O}}^{-}})},\,\,{{F}^{-}}\]

{Tip: More electronegative the element, higher is hard base character}.

Soft base : Which has more tendency to donate lone pair of electrons. $-{{\text{S}}^{-}},{{\text{S}}^{2-}},-\underset{1}{\mathop{{{\text{P}}^{\odot }}}}\,$

Generally, hard acids react with hard base and soft acids reacts with soft base.

concepts.title: Nucleophilicity and Basicity
concepts.conceptBody:
Nucleophilicity and Basicity

Nucleophilicity: It is the tendency to attack on electron deficient atom.

Higher the K, higher the nucleophilicity.

Basicity: It is the tendency to abstract a proton

\[{{B}^{-}}+{{H}_{2}}O\rightleftharpoons BH+O{{H}^{-}}\]

In comparing molecules with the same attacking atom, there is generally a direct relationship between basicity and Nucleophilicity. Stronger bases are better nucleophiles .

concepts.title: Trends in Nucleophilicity
concepts.conceptBody:
Trends in Nucleophilicity

(1) Species with a negative charge are stronger nucleophiles than analogous species without a negative charge. (Bases are always stronger nucleophiles than their conjugate acids).

$^{-}\text{OH}>{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{O}{{\quad }^{-}}\text{SH}>{{\text{H}}_{2}}~\text{S}{{\quad }^{-}}\text{N}{{\text{H}}_{2}}>\text{N}{{\text{H}}_{3}}$

(2) Nucleophilicity decreases from left to right across the periodic table. (The more electronegative elements hold on more tightly to their non-bonding electrons).

$^{-}\text{OH}>{{\text{F}}^{-}}\quad :\text{N}{{\text{H}}_{3}}>{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{O}:\quad {{\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}} \right)}_{3}}\text{P}>{{\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}} \right)}_{2}}~\text{S}$

(3) Nucleophilicity increases down the periodic table}\text{. (Increase in polarizability and size).

$\begin{matrix} {{\text{I}}^{-}}>\text{B}{{\text{r}}^{-}}>\text{C}{{\text{l}}^{-}}>{{\text{F}}^{-}} & \text{HS}{{\text{e}}^{-}}>\text{H}{{\text{S}}^{-}}>\text{H}{{\text{O}}^{-}} \\ {{\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}} \right)}_{3}}\text{P}>{{\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}} \right)}_{3}}~\text{N} & {} \\ \end{matrix}$

whereas basicity decreases down the group.

$\therefore \quad {{\text{I}}^{-}},\text{B}{{\text{r}}^{-}},\text{C}{{\text{l}}^{-}},{{\text{F}}^{-}}$

$[\begin{align} & \xleftarrow[{}]{\text{increasing mucleophiticity}} \\ & \,\,\,\,\,\,\xleftarrow[{}]{\text{decreasing basicity}} \\ \end{align}$

concepts.title: Steric Effect
concepts.conceptBody:
Steric Effects:

In general, the steric bulk has a detrimental effect on nucleophilicity.

Since nucleophilicity involves the attack of the nucleophile at a carbon center, large groups tend to hinder this process.

concepts.title: Solubility
concepts.conceptBody:
Solubility and Role of Solvent

Rule of thumb: Like Dissolves Like 

This means that reactants dissolve in solvents of similar polarity i.e., non polar or weakly polar dissolve in weakly polar solvents only.

That is the reason why hydrocarbons and alklyl halides do not dissolve in water, whose molecules are high polar and held together by strong hydrogen bonding.

Some terms: 

  • Hydrophilic (water loving) i.e. soluble in water
  • Hydrophobic/lilophilic (water hating) i.e. very less soluble in water as compared to solubility in non polar solvents

Note: As the number of carbon increases, the solubility decreases.

$\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{OH}>\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{OH}>\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}} \right)\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{OH}>\ldots .>\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}{{\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}} \right)}_{\text{n}}}-\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{OH}$

concepts.title: Polar Protic Solvent
concepts.conceptBody:
Nature of Solvents

  • Though there can be two more categories, i.e., weakly polar aprotic and non polar solvents but we will constraint our explanation to the above 2 categories only.

1. Polor Protic Solvents

These are solvents containing hydrogen that is attached to oxygen or nitrogen and hence acidic enough to form hydrogen bonds. In short, protic solvents are ones which have acidic hydrogen like${{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{O}$, methanol etc.

How they work: 

Substrate contains both cations and anions. Here in protic solvents, Cations are attracted to negative pole of polar solvent. In ${{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{O}$, negative part is the oxygen atom, as it is most electronegative and also has unshared lone pair.

To add to this, $\text{O}$ is attached with tiny hydrogen atoms which makes oxygen well exposed without crowding it.

Whereas,

Anions are attracted to positive pole of polar solvent which is hydrogen in case of ${{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{O}$, thus forming hydrogen bonds.

Case of ${{\mathbf{H}}_{\mathbf{2}}}\mathbf{O}$

concepts.title: Polar Aprotic Solvent
concepts.conceptBody:
2. Polar Aprotic Solvents

These are solvents which do not have acidic hydrogen i.e. hydrogen is not attached to electronegative $\text{O}$ or $\text{N}$.

Common example of such solvents:

How they work: 

They also dissolve ionic compounds but their action is completely different from protic solvent. Since they do not have acidic hydrogen they are not able to Solvate anions. Though they do solute cations by their electro-negative part.

So only this effect takes place.

Key to success

  • For ionic/polar substrate, the more solvated the cations and anions, faster is the reaction.

$\Rightarrow \quad $ Polar protic solvents will favour ionic reactants

i.e., SN1 mechanism (as carbocations are formed in the process)

  • Solvation differs from ion to ion, for ex in gaseous state, reactivity/basicity of halides is ${{\text{F}}^{-}}$ $>\text{C}{{\text{l}}^{-}}>\text{B}{{\text{r}}^{-}}>{{\text{I}}^{-}}$

but when we talk of protic solvents, the order reverses i.e. ${{\text{I}}^{-}}>\text{B}{{\text{r}}^{-}}>\text{C}{{\text{l}}^{-}}>{{\text{F}}^{-}}$

Why?: 

Since $\text{F}$ is a small atom, hence the Charge is concentrated in a small space & hence it is able to form hydrogen bonding at a very large scale as compared to that of ${{\text{I}}^{-}}$which has charge over a large area & hence weak hydrogen bonding.

Same reasoning can be given for, $\text{L}{{\text{i}}^{+}}\,\,\And \text{ N}{{\text{a}}^{+}}$. Again, in Aprotic solvents, since here is no formation of hydrogen bonding, hence order remains the same i.e ${{\text{F}}^{-}}>\text{C}{{\text{l}}^{-}}>\text{B}{{\text{r}}^{-}}>{{\text{I}}^{-}}$

So,

Tip : Common polar protic solvents

Common polar Aprotic solvents

Summing up the halogen series

concepts.title: Nucleophilic Substitution Reaction
concepts.conceptBody: Nucleophilic Substitution \[\mathbf{(}{{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{N}}}\mathbf{)}\]

concepts.title: SN2 Reaction Mechanism
concepts.conceptBody:
Second Order/Bimolecular nucleophilic Substitution $\mathbf{(S}{{\mathbf{N}}_{\mathbf{2}}}\mathbf{)}$

$C{{H}_{3}}C{{H}_{2}}Cl+{{\,}^{-}}OH\to C{{H}_{3}}C{{H}_{2}}OH+C{{l}^{-}}$

Mechanism: 

 

$^{-}OH$ shifts H to backside i.e. the site left by $C{{l}^{-}}.$

Hence, $\text{S}{{\text{N}}_{2}}$ leads to inversion of configuration , but only when the same priority group is replaced.

Note: It does not lead to change in d-l configuration.

Energy profile of the Reaction

The transition state is a point of highest energy (not an intermediate).

Kinetic information tells us that the rate is doubled when the $\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{Cl}$ also doubled when the $\left[ \text{H}{{\text{O}}^{-}} \right]$is doubled.

The rate is first order w.r.t. both reactants and is therefore 2 nd order overall.

Rate \(=\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{r}}\left[\mathrm{CH}_3 \mathrm{CH}_2 \mathrm{Cl}\right]\left[\mathrm{HO}^{-}\right]\)

The rate and mechanism are consistent since the mechanism requires a collision between the hydroxide ion and methyl iodide. Both species are present in the transition state, and the frequency of collisions is proportional to the concentrations of the reactants.

${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ = substitution, nucleophilic, bimolecular

Bimolecular means that the transition state of the RDS involves the collision of two molecules (Bimolecular reactions generally have 2nd order overall rate equations).

concepts.title: Leaving Group Effect
concepts.conceptBody:
Nucleophile Strength

The rate of the ${{S}_{N}}2$ reaction strongly depends on the nature of the nucleophile - a good nucleophile gives faster rates than a worse nucleophile.

Consider methanol $\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{OH} \right)$ and methoxide $\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}{{\text{O}}^{-}} \right)$reacting with $\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{I}$. It is found that methoxide reacts about a million times faster in ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ reactions than methanol.

Generally negatively charged species are much better nucleophiles than analogous neutral species. The two transition states are different energetically.

The T.S. with methoxide has the negative charge shared over the oxygen atom and the leaving halide.

In the methanol case, there is no negative charge. The halide has a partial negative charge and the oxygen has a partial positive charge. This is of higher energy.

Substrate Effects 

  • Leaving group effects
  • steric effects

(1) Leaving group effects 

A good leaving group has the following features:

(1) Electron withdrawing (to polarize the $\text{C}-\text{X}$ bond, making the $\text{C}$ electrophilic).

(2) Stable once it has left (not a strong base).

(3) Polarizable (to stabilize the T.S. - like ${{\text{I}}^{-}}$previously)

Common leaving groups: 

(ions) $\text{C}{{\text{l}}^{-}};\text{B}{{\text{r}}^{-}},{{\text{I}}^{-}},\text{RSO}_{3}^{-}$(sulfonate), $\text{RSO}_{4}^{-}$(sulfate), $\text{RPO}_{4}^{-}$(phosphate)

(neutral) ${{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{O},\text{R}-\text{OH},{{\text{R}}_{3}}~\text{N},{{\text{R}}_{3}}\text{P}$

Hydroxide ions are not good leaving groups (strong bases), but in acidic media, the

$\text{O gets protonated, and now }{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{O can serve as a good leaving group}\text{. }$

Neutral molecules can be good leaving groups from positively charged electrophiles. But the need to protonate the electrophile first limits the choice of nucleophiles to those that are not strong bases, since the nucleophile would simply get protonated.

concepts.title: Steric Effect of Substrate
concepts.conceptBody:
Steric Effects of the Substrate 

Large groups on the electrophile hinder the approach of the nucleophile.

Rel. rates for ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2:\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{X}>1>2>3$ alkyl halides

For an ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ reaction, the nucleophile must approach the small backside lobe of the $\text{C}-\text{X}$ s${{\text{p}}^{3}}$ orbital. Generally, one alkyl group slows the reaction, two alkyl groups make it difficult three alkyl close to impossible.

Thus decreasing reactivity by ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$

Effect of Solvent on \[{{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{N}}}\mathbf{2}\]

concepts.title: Energy Profile Diagram
concepts.conceptBody:
Energy Profile

Rate of reaction increases only when

(1) If ${{\text{H}}_{\text{TS}}}$ decreases (this is because less energy would be required to reach the transition state)

(2) If ${{\text{H}}_{\text{GS}}}$ increases

(3) If both of the above occur simultaneously.

Some applications

(a) $\text{MeI}{{+}^{-}}\text{OH}\xrightarrow{{}}\text{MeOH}+{{\text{I}}^{-}}$

(b) \[M{{e}^{-}}{{S}^{+}}\,M{{e}_{2}}+{{\,}^{-}}OH\to MeOH+S\,M{{e}_{2}}\]

(c) \[MeI+N{{H}_{3}}\to M{{e}^{+}}N{{H}_{2}}+{{I}^{-}}\]

In case of (a) and (b), reacting mixture has full charges whereas transition state has partial negative charges.

$\therefore \quad $ Reacting species will be more solvated. Hence ${{\text{H}}_{\text{Gs}}}$ will decrease more than ${{\text{H}}_{\text{Ts}}}$ with the introduction of protic solvent.

Whereas in (c) reacting mixture is charge free and in transition state some partial charge has developed. Therefore, Ts will be more solvated. Thus ${{\text{H}}_{\text{Ts}}}$ decreases more than ${{\text{H}}_{\text{Gs}}}$ in this case.

concepts.title: SN1 Reaction Mechanism
concepts.conceptBody:
First order Nucleophilic Substitution $\left( {{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{N}}}\mathbf{1} \right)$

There is also an ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ reaction. (Substitution, nucleophilic, unimolecular)

Consider the reaction of t-butylbromide and methanol:

${{\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}} \right)}_{3}}\text{C}-\text{Br}+\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}-\text{OH}\to {{\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}} \right)}_{3}}\text{C}-\text{O}-\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}+\text{H}-\text{Br}$

The rate was found to depend only on the concentration of t-butylbromide.

$\text{ Rate }={{\text{k}}_{\text{r}}}\left[ {{\left( \text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}} \right)}_{3}}\text{C}-\text{Br} \right]$

The rate is first order overall - unimolecular

It appears that the nucleophile is not present in the R.D.S. (rate determining step), but must react somewhere after the R.D.S. has occurred.

Mechanism: 

Step 1: Formation of carbocation (R.D.S.)

Step 2a: Nucleophilic Attack

Step 2 (b): Loss of a proton

The ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ reaction is a two step process, with the first being a slow ionization reaction generating a carbocation.

The second is the quick nucleophilic attack by the nucleophile on the carbocation. (In some case, like when water or alcohol is the nucleophile, a quick loss of a proton gives the final product).

$\Rightarrow \quad $ Solvation assists the ionization process, since the energy of activation required for breaking of the bond is largely recovered for solvation of ions produced.

In general:

\(\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{R}-\mathrm{X} \rightarrow \mathrm{R}^{+}+\mathrm{X}^{-} \text {(R.D.S., slow) } \\ & \mathrm{R}^{+}+\mathrm{Nuc}^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{R}-\mathrm{Nuc}~(\text {fast})\end{aligned}\)

 

The ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ reaction has two transition states, whereas the ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ only has one transition state. Consequently, ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ rates depend on carbocation stability.

Since alkyl groups are known to stabilize carbocations (inductive effects and hyperconjugation), ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ reactivities decrease in the order of:

$3>2>1>\text{ methyl cation }$

(This is the opposite for${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$reactivity).

Resonance stabilized cation are also important for${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ reactivity, for example, allyl bromide is much more reactive than other primary halides in ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ reactions.

Leaving Group Effects

In the R.D.S. for an ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ reaction, the bond to the leaving group is breaking therefore a highly polarizable leaving group helps stabilize the T.S. through partial bonding as it leaves (like for ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ case).

The leaving group should be stable after it has left with the bonding electrons, and also be a weak base.

The leaving group starts to take on partial negative charge as the cation starts to form. Good leaving groups are essential for both ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ and ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ reactions.

Solvent Effects

The R.D.S. of an ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ reaction involves the formation of 2 ions, therefore polar solvents (which stabilize ions) enhance ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ reactivities.

Protic solvents are especially useful since the hydrogen bonding stabilizes the anionic leaving group after ionization.

concepts.title: Stereochemistry and Rearrangement in SN1 Reaction
concepts.conceptBody:
Stereochemistry of the ${{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{N}}}\mathbf{1}$ Reaction

(Recall that the ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ reaction is stereospecific, always proceeding with inversion).

The ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ reaction is not stereospecific.

Consider the reaction below:

The carbocation produced is planar and $\text{s}{{\text{p}}^{2}}$ hybridized.

If the nucleophile attacks from the side that the leaving group is attached, the product displays retention of configuration. So, ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ leads to reacemization.

concepts.title: Nucleophilic Reaction Mechanism
concepts.conceptBody:
Rearrangements in ${{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{N}}}\mathbf{1}$ Reactions

Carbocations will often undergo rearrangements , producing more stable ions.

For example the products of the ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ reaction of 2-bromo-3-methylbutane and ethanol are a mixture of structural isomers - the expected product and a rearranged product.

The two products arise from the same carbocation. In one case the cation is trapped by the nucleophile before it can rearrange, whereas the second product arises by quenching of the rearranged cation by the nucleophile.

Mechanism: 

Step 1 : Formation of carbocation:

Step 2: Attack of solvent before and after rearrangement.

(Rearrangements do not occur in ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ reactions since carbocations are not intermediates).

concepts.title: SN1 vs SN2 Reaction Mechanism
concepts.conceptBody:
${{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{N}}}\mathbf{1 vs }{{\mathbf{S}}_{\mathbf{N}}}\mathbf{2}$

Which mechanism the reaction will follow is decided upon the following 4 factors i.e.

1. Nature of substrate

2. Strength of Nucleophile

3. Nature of leaving group

4. Role of solvent

We will now see the affect of each of these factors.

1. Nature of Substrate

$\text{ For }2\text{ RX we will have to see for more factors }$

2. Strength of Nucleophile

“for ${{\text{S}}_{{\underset{\scriptscriptstyle-}{N}}}}\underset{\scriptscriptstyle-}{2}$. key to success is the attack of nucleophile”.

So, generally,

$\text{weak N}{{\text{u}}^{-}}:{{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$

$\text{strong N}{{\text{u}}^{-}}:{{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$

Here in ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}$, the effect of steric hindrance also has to be taken in count.

  • In case, there is not much hindrance, nucleophile can attack easily.

Now it has 2 alkyl groups present which shows some hindrance. Hence nucleophile has to be a strong one so as to attack the carbon & go for ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ attack.

Nucleophilicity vs Basicity

In general $\text{N}{{\text{u}}^{-}}$& basic character run in parallel but their order is reversed in the same group of periodic table.

$\begin{align} & {{I}^{-}},\,\,B{{r}^{-}},\,\,C{{l}^{-}},\,\,{{F}^{-}} \\ & \xleftarrow[{}]{\text{nuelceophilicity}} \\ & \,\,\,\,\,\xrightarrow[{}]{basicity} \\ \end{align}$

Nucleophilicity is a function of polarizability. And bigger the size, greater is polarizability. And a better nucleophile favours substitution, whereas base favours elimination, which we will deal later.

Note: $\text{N}{{\text{u}}^{+}}$does not play an important role in ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ because it does not play any role in rate determining step.

3. Nature of Leaving group

For substitution, either ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ or ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ the presence of a good leaving facilitates the reaction.

A good leaving group 

eg. ${{\text{I}}^{-}}$is a good leaving group because its a weak base. It is a weak base because its a conjugate base of a strong acid HI.

(a) will more readily go for substitution as compared to (b) as ${{\text{I}}^{-}}$is a better leaving group than $\text{C}{{\text{l}}^{-}}$.

$\begin{matrix} RI\,>\,\,RBr>\,\,RCl>\,\,RF \\ \xrightarrow[order\,\,of\,\,substitution]{decrea\sin g} \\ \end{matrix}$

concepts.title: Elimination Reaction
concepts.conceptBody:
Elimination/Dehydrohalogenation

Also known as 1-2 elimination. This mechanism involves the elimination of the halogen atom and hydrogen atom from carbon adjacent to the one losing the halogen to form alkene.

Elimination $\to $ loss of $\beta $-hydrogen

$\alpha -$ carbon $\to $ where halogen is attached

$\beta -$ carbon $\to $ carbon adjacent to $\alpha $-carbon

$\beta -$ hydrogen $\to $ hydrogen attached to $\beta $-carbon

Note: Reaction is brought about by action of base only.

Before we go into details of 2 mechanisms governing eliminations i.e. ${{\text{E}}_{1}}$, & ${{\text{E}}_{2}}$, first do a rule known as ‘SAYTZEFF RULE’ for alkenes.

concepts.title: Saytzeff Rule
concepts.conceptBody:
Saytzeff Rule

It says that in alkenes, the alkene with greater number of alkyl groups attached to the doubly bonded carbon atom is more stable and hence will be major product for example.

Ease of formation of alkenes

${{\text{R}}_{2}}\text{C}=\text{C}{{\text{R}}_{2}}>{{\text{R}}_{2}}\text{C}=\text{CHR}>\text{RCH}=\text{CHR}>{{\text{R}}_{2}}\text{CH}=\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}>\text{RCH}=\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}>\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}=\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}$

In dehydrohalogenation, the more stable the alkene the faster it is formed. Elimination Mechanism

Elimination can follow two mechanisms

  • E1 mechanism
  • E2 mechanism

Let us do them in detail separately.

concepts.title: E2 Reaction Mechanism
concepts.conceptBody:
${{\mathbf{E}}_{\mathbf{2}}}$ Mechanism

As the name suggest, E2 follows second order kinetics. This means that the rate is dependent upon the concentration of 2 substances:

1. Alkyl Hallide

2. Base

$\text{rate}=\text{k}[\text{RX}][:\text{B}]$

Hence is it also known as Bimolecular elimination.

How it occurs?

E2 like ${{\text{S}}_{{{\text{N}}^{2}}}}$ is a single step reaction.

Bonds to hydrogen and the leaving groups are partly broken bond. Double bond is partly formed in transition state. All these things are taking place simultaneously.

Factors that stabilize the alkene, also stabalizes the transition state as it is already partly alkene.

There are 2 factors that-we look while talking about the stability of alkenes.

1. Saytzeff rule

2. Hoffman rule

We have already discussed Saytzeff rule, & we will discuss Hoffman rule a bit later (Hoffman rule is opposite of Saytzeff Rule)

Since the transition state depends upon the stability of alkene, hence substituted alkenes are more stable and hence the order of dehydrohalogenation becomes

$3>2>1$

concepts.title: E1 Reaction Mechanism
concepts.conceptBody:
${{\mathbf{E}}_{1}}$ Mechanism

As the name suggest it is first order kinetics and analogous to ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$.

here bond breaking & bond formation are same as in $\text{E}2$, however it happens in two steps rather than just one step as in E1.

E1

(Unimolecular elimination)

Step 1: 

 

Step 2: 

 

Here step 1 is identical to as in ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}^{1}$, where the formation of carbocation takes place & in step 2, carbocation reacts with base to yield elimination product, whereas in ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}^{1}$ carbocation reacted with nucleophile to yield substituted product.

Here again the first step is the rate determining step.

$\therefore \quad \text{r}=\text{ rate }=\text{k}[\text{RX}]$

i.e. rate is dependent only on the concentration of substrate and independent of base concentration.

You can see that there are so many similarities between $\text{E}1\,\,\And \,\,~{{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ mechanisms

$\therefore \quad $ Wherever E1 can occur there will be a possibility of ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}^{1}$ also. We will discuss how to eliminate this confusion later.

Reactivity in E1: $3>2>1$

because you have to check for stabality of carbocation in E1.

Orientation in E1: Again here saytzeff rule comes into play. Later on we will also see how Hoffman rule affects the orientation.

Let us take an example to understand the mechanism.

concepts.title: E2 vs E1 Reaction Mechanism
concepts.conceptBody:
E2 Vs E1 

How to figure out which elimination mechanism is favourable when the order of both mechanisms is

$3>2>1$

  • The stronger the base, the more E2 is favoured over E1.

Why

$\to $ Because E1 mechanism is independent of base and E2 mechanism depends on the concentration of base.

  • Polar medium favours E1, whereas Non polar medium favours E2 This is analogous to${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}^{1}$ and ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}^{2}$. Though this effect is not that affective
  • Bulky base favours E2.

{TIP: alc. $\text{KOH}$ is classical reagent for elimination\}

  • E1 mechanism is encountered only with secondary and tertiary substractes or where base is of low concentration or weak or where base is the solvent i.e. SOLVOLYSIS.

In these cases “HOFFMAN RULE” is followed, which is anti-saytzeff rule. i.e. less substituted alkene is the main product.

concepts.title: Intermolecular and Intramolecular Reactions
concepts.conceptBody:
Intermolecular And Intramolecular Reactions:

When a molecule has 2 functional group, also known as bifunctional molecule, two kind of reactions are possible.

Let us take an example to understand these 2 mechanisms.

Intermolecular reaction :

Here molecules of the same compound combine together to give inter molecular reaction.

Intramolecular Reaction:

Inter vs Intra-molecular reactions:

  • Intra molecular reactions are prefered when Rings formed are stable
  • 5-6 member rings are stable and hence favour intra mechanism.
  • EXCEPTION: 3 membered rings are also stable and hence show intra mechanism.

For intermolecular

$\Rightarrow $ If ring formation occurs in the form of 4 membered ring or greater than 6 membered rings, then ring formation is discarded & inter molecular reaction takes place.

Note: 

6 membered ring is more stable than 5 or 3 membered ring. So given the option 6 membered ring will be the major product in reaction.

Some examples of intramolecular reactions

concepts.title: Ambient Nucleophiles
concepts.conceptBody:
Ambident Nucleophiles

Some nucleophiles have lone pair of electrons on more than one atom and can attack through more than one site. Such nucleophiles are called ambident nucleophiles. In such cases, different products are possible due to attack through different sites. Attack by a specific site can be promoted under special conditions. Two well-known examples are discussed in detail.

Attack by CN - nucleophile \[\mathbf{(}{{\mathbf{:}}^{\mathbf{-}}}\mathbf{C}\equiv \mathbf{N}\]:)

$\text{R}-\text{N}\xrightarrow{C{{N}^{-}}}\underset{\text{ nitriles }}{\mathop{\text{R}-\text{CN}}}\,+\underset{\text{ isonitriles }}{\mathop{\text{R}-\text{NC}}}\,+{{\text{X}}^{-}}$

In $\text{C}{{\text{N}}^{-}}$, carbon (negatively charged) will be a soft base as compared to nitrogen. So, if the reaction proceeds via ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ mechanism, which produces a free carbocation (a hard acid), then attack through nitrogen (hard base) will take place. But if the reaction proceeds via ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ mechanism (small positively charged carbon is soft acid) then attack through carbon (soft base) will take place. So, if we want to increase relative yield of nitriles, we can use $\text{NaCN}$ or KCN etc. in a less polar solvent, which facilitates ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ substitution. Similarly, if we want to increase the yield of isonitriles, we can use $\text{AgCN}$. $\text{A}{{\text{g}}^{+}}$has very strong affinity for ${{\text{X}}^{-}}$, so it favours the formation of ${{\text{R}}^{+}}$and the reaction proceeds via ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}^{1}$ mechanism. This will result in attack by hard base given R-NC. Further if we compare primary, secondary and tertiary alkyl halides, formation of R-NC should be favoured due to more favourable ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ substituion in tertiary alkyl halide. But the exception is that tertiary alkyl halides undergo elimination and the yield decreases. This is because $\text{C}{{\text{N}}^{-}}$is a strong base, which can also cause elimination reaction.

Attack by $\mathbf{NO}_{\mathbf{2}}^{\mathbf{-}}$nucleophile ${{(}^{-}}\mathbf{O}-\mathbf{N=O})$

$\text{R}-\text{X}\xrightarrow{NO_{2}^{-}}\underset{\text{ alkane nitrite }}{\mathop{\text{R}-\text{O}-\text{N}=\text{O}}}\,+\underset{\text{ nitro alkane }}{\mathop{\text{R}-\text{N}{{\text{O}}_{2}}}}\,+{{\text{X}}^{-}}$

In $\text{NO}_{2}^{-}$, oxygen (negatively charged) will be a hard base as compared to nitrogen. So, if the reaction proceeds via ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ mechanism, then attack through oxygen (hard base) will take place to produce alkane nitrite. But if the reaction takes place via ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ mechanism then attack through nitrogen (soft base) takes place to give nitro alkane.

If we want to increase the yield of nitro alkane, the reaction should proceed via ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ mechanism, i.e. we can use $\text{NaN}{{\text{O}}_{2}},\text{KN}{{\text{O}}_{2}}$ etc. Moreover, the yield will be best if we use primary alkyl halide and less polar solvent. Formation of nitrite will dominate, if we use tertiary alkyl halide, more polar solvent and $\text{AgN}{{\text{O}}_{2}}$ because $\text{A}{{\text{g}}^{+}}$has strong affinity for ${{\text{X}}^{-}}$and can form a carbocation to force the reaction to proceed via ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}1$ mechanism. Primary alkyl halide with $\text{AgN}{{\text{O}}_{2}}$ chiefly gives nitro alkane but if secondary and tertiary alkyl halides are used then $\text{AgN}{{\text{O}}_{2}}$ will yield nitrite as the major product.

concepts.title: Finkelstein Reaction
concepts.conceptBody:
Finkelstein Reaction

$\text{R}-\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}-\text{X}\underset{\text{MX}}{\mathop{\overset{\text{M}{{\text{X}}^{\prime }}}{\mathop{\rightleftharpoons }}\,}}\,\text{R}-\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}-{{\text{X}}^{\prime }}$

Treatment of a primary alkyl halide or pseudohalide with an alkali metal halide (e.g. KF, KI) leads to replacement of the halogen via an${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ Reaction.

The classic case of finkelstein reaction includes the conversion of alkyl chloride or bromide to alkyl iodide in presence of sodium iodide in acetone

$\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{Br}\xrightarrow[Acetone]{Na1}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{3}}\text{C}{{\text{H}}_{2}}\text{I}+\text{NaBr}$

The equilibrium position of the reaction depends on the nucleophilicity of the anion, whether a good leaving group is present, and whether one anion is better stabilized than the other in a given solvent. For example, reactions with KF will thus lead cleanly to fluoroalkanes, because fluoride is such a poor leaving group due to the stability of the C-F bond.

In general, the reaction is run with an excess of the metal halide. The use of metal salts that have a high lattice energy require the addition of a crown ether.

The equilibrium position of the reaction also depends on the solubility of the metal salt in the solvent used. Thus, the substitution of bromo-and chloroalkanes with KI in acetone leads cleanly to the desired iodoalkane products, since $\text{KCl}$ and $\text{KBr}$ are insoluble in acetone and are consequently removed from the equilibrium:

\[R-C{{H}_{2}}-Cl\xrightarrow[Acetone]{KI}R-C{{H}_{2}}-I\]

concepts.title: Wurtz Reaction
concepts.conceptBody:
Reactions of Alkyl Halide

Wurtz reaction

It is a coupling reaction whereby two alkyl halides are reacted with sodium to form a new carbon-carbon bond:

$2\text{R}-\text{X}+2\text{Na}\xrightarrow{{}}\text{R}-\text{R}+2\text{N}{{\text{a}}^{+}}{{\text{X}}^{-}}$

The related reaction dealing with aryl halides is called the Wurtz-Fitting reaction.

Limitations

The Wurtz reaction is limited to the synthesis of symmetric alkanes. If two dissimilar alkyl halides are taken as reactants, then the product is a mixture of alkanes that is, often, difficult to separate. Since the reaction involves free radical species, a side reaction also occurs to produce an alkene. This side-reaction becomes more significant when the alkyl halides are bulky at the halogen-attached carbon. This is because the activation energy required for the ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ reaction in the second step becomes significantly high, so the alternate elimination mechanism is favored.

Mechanism 

This reaction involves the radical species $\stackrel{\bullet}{\text{R}}$.

One electron from sodium is transferred to the halogen to produce a sodium halide and an alkyl radical.

$\text{R}-\text{X}+\text{Na}\xrightarrow{{}}\stackrel{\bullet}{\text{R}} +\text{N}{{\text{a}}^{+}}{{\text{X}}^{-}}$

The alkyl radical then accepts an electron from another sodium atom to form an alkyl anion and the sodium becomes cationic.

$\stackrel{\bullet}{\text{R}} +\text{Na}\xrightarrow{{}}{{\text{R}}^{-}}\text{N}{{\text{a}}^{+}}$

The alkyl anion then displaces the halide in an ${{\text{S}}_{\text{N}}}2$ reaction, forming a new carbon-carbon covalent bond.

$\text{R}-\text{N}{{\text{a}}^{+}}+\text{R}-\text{X}\xrightarrow{{}}\text{R}-\text{R}+\text{N}{{\text{a}}^{+}}{{\text{X}}^{-}}$
